name: OWASP Amass
purpose: Network-mapping tool that performs attack-surface discovery through DNS enumeration, certificate transparency, web archives, API sources and optional active probing, building a graph of an organisation's internet assets.
journalism_use_case: Mapping the internet footprint of an organisation under investigation: a surveillance vendor's subdomains, staging environments, mail infrastructure and related domains — which reveals products, partners and sometimes customers that the public website does not mention.
pros: Breadth of passive sources (certificate transparency, web archives, DNS datasets) means substantial discovery without touching the target, which is the right operational-security posture
Builds a graph rather than a flat list, so relationships between assets are visible — useful for distinguishing a company's own infrastructure from a shared host
OWASP project with institutional governance and a long track record, so it is not a weekend tool
Forgotten staging and development subdomains are a recurring source of investigative material, and systematic enumeration is how you find them
cons: Active enumeration modes send traffic to the target and are detectable; defaults need deliberate configuration if you do not want to announce your interest
Security-tooling heritage means the framing is penetration testing, and aggressive use against an organisation you do not have authorisation to test raises legal questions in some jurisdictions
Some data sources require API keys, several of them paid, so full capability has a cost the free tool hides
Output volume is large and noisy; separating the organisation's real assets from shared-hosting neighbours takes judgement
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under OWASP project governance. Amass is a standard tool in attack-surface discovery, which is well established in the security community.
assessment: Adopt it for infrastructure mapping with passive sources only as the default — the passive discovery alone is usually enough and leaves no trace with the target. For your profile the sequence that works is Amass for enumeration, certificate transparency for ongoing monitoring, and RIR records for authoritative ownership before any published claim. Get a view on the legal position for active scanning in your jurisdiction before enabling it against a company.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under OWASP project governance with ongoing development. Maintenance assessed on activity and institutional backing; the project has a long continuous history.
licence: Apache-2.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Third-party data sources have their own terms; several require API keys.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published. The constraints are legal (active scanning) and contractual (data-source API terms) rather than licence-based.
costs: No fee. Several optional data sources require paid API keys (prices vary; not verified here). Compute is modest. Estimate.
privacy: Passive modes leave no trace with the target. Active modes are visible. Queries to third-party data sources disclose the organisations you are mapping to those providers.
alternatives: subfinder for faster passive subdomain enumeration with less breadth
Metabigor for keyless public-source footprinting
certstream plus crt.sh for certificate-based discovery alone
blockers: Active scanning modes are detectable and may engage computer-misuse law
summary: Network-mapping tool that performs attack-surface discovery through DNS enumeration, certificate transparency, web archives…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: subfinder
purpose: Fast passive subdomain-enumeration tool that queries many online sources — certificate transparency, DNS datasets, search engines, scan databases — and returns discovered subdomains.
journalism_use_case: The quick first step in mapping a target's infrastructure: enumerate a surveillance vendor's or front company's subdomains in seconds from passive sources, which frequently surfaces product names, customer portals and regional deployments.
pros: Passive-only by design, so it leaves no trace with the target — the correct default for investigating an organisation that would react to being probed
Very fast and composable: it does one thing and pipes into httpx or your own tooling, which fits a scripted workflow
MIT licensed and actively maintained by an organisation with consistent release discipline across its tool suite
No API keys needed for useful results, though adding them widens coverage
cons: Subdomains only, so it is one dimension of infrastructure mapping — Amass gives you the broader graph
Coverage depends on third-party sources, so results vary over time and an absent subdomain means nothing
Queries disclose the domains you are enumerating to the data sources, several of which are commercial
Security-tooling context means the documentation assumes penetration-testing framing
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under ProjectDiscovery's maintenance, consistent with the release discipline observed across their other tools in this catalogue (katana, uncover).
assessment: Adopt it as the fast first pass before Amass — seconds of passive enumeration often answers the question, and only if it does not do you need the heavier tool. For your profile the practical chain is subfinder to enumerate, httpx to see what responds, and manual review of anything unexpected; staging and admin subdomains are where the interesting material is, and they are usually found in the first thirty seconds.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under ProjectDiscovery's maintenance, whose other tools in this catalogue (katana, uncover) show same-day commits and regular releases — a consistent organisational pattern.
model_or_data_licence: Third-party data sources have their own terms.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. Data-source terms apply to API-key-based sources.
costs: No fee. Optional API keys for wider coverage, some paid (not priced here). Negligible compute.
privacy: Passive with respect to the target. The data sources learn which domains you enumerate.
alternatives: Amass for broader infrastructure graphing
crt.sh queries for certificate-transparency-only discovery
Metabigor for ASN and netblock mapping rather than subdomains
summary: Fast passive subdomain-enumeration tool that queries many online sources — certificate transparency, DNS datasets…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure

name: httpx
purpose: Fast multi-purpose HTTP toolkit that probes a list of hosts and reports status codes, titles, technologies, certificates, response hashes and screenshots.
journalism_use_case: Turning a list of discovered hostnames into a picture of what is actually running: which of a vendor's two hundred subdomains respond, what their page titles say, which share a TLS certificate — the triage step that identifies the handful worth looking at by hand.
pros: Page titles and certificate details at scale are remarkably informative: a title like 'Lawful Interception Management Console' on a staging subdomain is the kind of finding that makes a story
Response hashing groups identical pages, which quickly separates real applications from parked-domain boilerplate
MIT licensed, very fast, and composes directly with subfinder and katana in a pipeline
Optional screenshots give a visual record of what was live at a point in time — useful evidence if the page disappears
cons: Active by nature: it sends requests to every host, so the target sees your probing — this is the step where passive reconnaissance becomes visible, and that should be a deliberate decision
Aggressive default concurrency can look hostile and may trip protections; rate limits need setting
Security-tooling framing, so the defaults and documentation assume authorised testing
Output needs interpretation: a 403 may mean an interesting restricted application or nothing at all
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived under ProjectDiscovery's maintenance, consistent with the organisation's observed release discipline.
assessment: Adopt it as the triage step after passive enumeration, with concurrency reduced and a deliberate decision that you are willing to be seen probing. For your profile the valuable practice is capturing screenshots and titles as evidence at the moment of probing, because an interesting staging subdomain tends to disappear shortly after someone notices it has been found. Route the traffic through an egress not attributable to your newsroom.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived under ProjectDiscovery's maintenance, consistent with same-day commit and regular release patterns observed across their suite in this catalogue.
licence_restrictions: Code unrestricted. Probing a third party's infrastructure may engage computer-misuse law depending on jurisdiction and intensity — a legal question to settle before use.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute; bandwidth proportional to the host list.
privacy: Active: the target sees your requests and can identify your IP and pattern. Use a dedicated egress and conservative rate limits.
alternatives: Manual browsing of the handful of hosts you most care about, which is slower and invisible
shot-scraper for screenshot capture with a browser rather than a security tool
Passive sources only, accepting that you learn less
blockers: Active probing is visible to the target and may engage computer-misuse law
summary: Fast multi-purpose HTTP toolkit that probes a list of hosts and reports status codes, titles, technologies, certificates…

name: dnstwist
purpose: Tool that generates and tests permutations of a domain name — typos, homoglyphs, character swaps, alternative TLDs — to find registered lookalike domains, with DNS, WHOIS and page-similarity checks.
journalism_use_case: Finding impersonation infrastructure aimed at your own outlet or at a story's subject: lookalike domains are used for phishing journalists and for publishing fake versions of news sites, and dnstwist finds the registered ones systematically rather than by accident.
pros: Directly protective as well as investigative: running it against your own domain finds the lookalikes being prepared to phish your staff or impersonate your publication, which is a realistic threat to exile media
Homoglyph detection catches the internationalised-domain tricks that are invisible to the eye, which is exactly how credential-phishing domains evade notice
Page-similarity checking distinguishes a parked typo-squat from an active clone of your site — the difference between noise and an incident
Long-established, widely packaged and MIT licensed
cons: Permutation generation produces a large candidate space, so results need filtering and most registered hits are commercial typo-squatting rather than targeted impersonation
DNS and WHOIS checks against many candidates are visible to resolvers and registries, and WHOIS data availability has degraded substantially under privacy rules
Finding a lookalike domain tells you it exists, not who registered it — attribution needs registrar records, certificate data or hosting analysis
Maintenance cadence is steady rather than brisk
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with a long history. dnstwist is a standard tool for lookalike-domain detection, well established in the security community.
assessment: Adopt it and run it on a schedule against your own domains — this is one of the few tools in the catalogue that protects you directly, and for a media-in-exile outlet impersonation and credential phishing are concrete rather than theoretical risks. Pair it with certificate-transparency monitoring, which catches lookalikes at the moment a certificate is issued, often before the site is live. Treat discovered domains as leads for attribution work.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with a long release history and steady rather than frequent updates. Classified stable-low: the permutation logic is mature and the tool is feature-complete for its purpose.
licence: Apache-2.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
costs: No fee. Negligible compute. Optional paid data sources for richer WHOIS or registration data (not priced here).
privacy: DNS and WHOIS lookups are visible to resolvers and registries. Checking your own domain's permutations discloses little of consequence; checking a target's may indicate interest.
alternatives: certstream monitoring for lookalike detection at certificate issuance — faster and fully passive
Commercial brand-protection services, which are more thorough and expensive
Manual registry searches for a specific suspected domain
summary: Tool that generates and tests permutations of a domain name — typos, homoglyphs, character swaps, alternative TLDs…

name: SSLyze
purpose: TLS and SSL configuration scanner that reports supported protocols, cipher suites, certificate chains, and known weaknesses, with a Python API and JSON output.
journalism_use_case: Two uses: documenting that an organisation handling sensitive citizen data runs demonstrably weak TLS — a concrete, checkable security-negligence finding — and examining certificate chains on suspected infrastructure to find shared issuance patterns that link hosts.
pros: Produces specific, verifiable technical findings: 'this government portal accepts a deprecated protocol' is a factual claim a reader can re-test, which is unusually solid ground for a technology story
Certificate-chain detail supports infrastructure attribution: shared intermediate certificates or unusual issuance patterns link hosts that otherwise look unrelated
Python API and JSON output make it scriptable across a list of targets, so a survey of a sector's TLS posture is feasible
Well-established with a long maintenance history and a focused scope
cons: Active scanning: each check connects to the target, so the target can see it — and scanning a government portal's TLS, while unremarkable, is still a visible act
Interpreting results requires TLS literacy: a 'weak' cipher may be present but unused, and publishing a misread finding would be embarrassing and correctable by the target
Narrow scope by design — it tells you about TLS configuration and nothing else
Findings age quickly as configurations change, so a published claim needs a date and ideally a saved JSON record
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with a long release history. SSLyze is a standard TLS assessment tool, well established in the security community.
assessment: Integrate it for the specific story type where it produces hard findings — the security posture of organisations holding sensitive data — and for certificate-based infrastructure linking. For your profile the publication discipline is to save the raw JSON with a timestamp, have someone TLS-literate review the interpretation, and give the organisation an opportunity to respond, since configurations can be fixed between your scan and publication and you want the record of what you found.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with a long release history and steady maintenance. Classified stable-low: a mature, focused tool where the pace reflects completeness.
licence: AGPL-3.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
licence_restrictions: Copyleft would apply to a modified network service built on it; immaterial for command-line use. Note that AGPL on a scanning tool is unusual and worth confirming if you embed it.
privacy: Active connections to the target, which are visible in its logs. Unremarkable for TLS assessment but still a disclosure of interest.
alternatives: testssl.sh as a shell-based alternative with similar coverage
Qualys SSL Labs for a hosted assessment, which discloses the target to a third party and produces a citable public report
Certificate transparency data for issuance patterns without connecting to the host
summary: TLS and SSL configuration scanner that reports supported protocols, cipher suites, certificate chains, and known weaknesses…

name: asn (nitefood)
purpose: Shell-based reconnaissance tool that resolves IP addresses, prefixes, ASNs and domains to network ownership, BGP routing, geolocation and reputation data, with bulk and interactive modes.
journalism_use_case: Answering 'who owns this address' quickly and from several sources: given an IP from a log, a certificate or a leaked document, establish the hosting provider, the announcing ASN and the responsible organisation — the attribution step that turns a technical artefact into a nameable entity.
pros: Aggregates several authoritative sources (RIR records, BGP data, geolocation) in one command, which is faster and less error-prone than consulting each by hand
Bulk mode means you can attribute a list of addresses from a log or a dataset in one pass, which is the realistic investigative need
Shell-based with no heavy dependencies, so it runs anywhere including a minimal container or a field machine
Covers the authoritative sources that matter for a published attribution claim (RIR allocation and BGP announcement) rather than only commercial geolocation
cons: Queries go to multiple third-party services, so your target addresses are disclosed to several providers — worth routing through a dedicated egress
IP geolocation is notoriously imprecise at city level and worse for mobile and cloud ranges, so a published location claim based on it is fragile
Shell-script architecture means error handling is basic and output parsing for automation is awkward
Small project; verify liveness and source availability before relying on it for a deadline
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived. The tool is known in the network-investigation community as a convenient aggregator; no journalism deployment verified.
assessment: Integrate it as the quick attribution step, with the discipline of confirming anything published against the RIR record directly — allocation data is authoritative and geolocation is not. For your profile the common error to avoid is publishing an IP geolocation as a location: for cloud and mobile addresses it is frequently wrong by hundreds of kilometres, and the defensible claim concerns who announces and who was allocated the range, not where a server physically sits.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with modest ongoing activity. Classified stable-low; because the capability depends on third-party source availability, verify it works before relying on it.
licence: MIT (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Third-party data sources have their own terms; RIR data is generally open.
licence_restrictions: Permissive as published; third-party service terms apply to automated querying.
costs: No fee. Negligible compute. Some data sources may rate-limit or require keys.
privacy: Queries disclose the addresses and domains you are investigating to several third-party services — more exposure than a single lookup, so use a dedicated egress for sensitive work.
alternatives: Direct RIR (RIPE, ARIN, APNIC) queries for authoritative allocation data
PyBGPStream for rigorous BGP analysis from public archives
Metabigor for organisation-level netblock and ASN mapping
summary: Shell-based reconnaissance tool that resolves IP addresses, prefixes, ASNs and domains to network ownership, BGP routing…

name: theHarvester
purpose: Reconnaissance tool that gathers names, email addresses, subdomains, hosts and open ports for a domain from search engines, certificate transparency, scan databases and other public sources.
journalism_use_case: Building a picture of an organisation's people and infrastructure from public sources: staff email patterns, subdomains and hosts for a company under investigation — which supports both contact research and infrastructure mapping from a single pass.
pros: Combines people and infrastructure discovery in one tool, which matches how an investigation into an organisation actually proceeds
Many sources queried in parallel, so coverage is broader than any single source gives
Long-established with a large community and wide packaging in security distributions
Email-pattern discovery is practically useful for contact research, where knowing an organisation's address format lets you reach a named individual
cons: Harvesting email addresses creates a personal-data collection with data-protection obligations, which reporters routinely overlook — this is the item that most needs a policy

Depends on search engines and third-party sources whose access has degraded substantially (the same anti-scraping pressure that killed automated dorking), so results are less complete than they once were
Several sources require API keys, some paid, so full capability has a hidden cost
Security-tooling framing, and aggressive use against an organisation raises the usual legal questions
feedback: No individual user reports verified in this survey. Documented from the metadata sweep: the repository is live and non-archived with a long history. The degradation of search-engine-based collection is corroborated by the independent findings on pagodo, dorks_hunter and Whoogle in this catalogue.
assessment: Integrate it with lowered expectations and a data-protection decision made in advance. For your profile two points matter. First, search-engine sources are much weaker than they were, so treat subfinder plus certificate transparency as the reliable infrastructure path and theHarvester as supplementary. Second, the harvested email list is regulated personal data: decide retention and protection before you run it, not after, because an undocumented list of an organisation's staff addresses sitting on a laptop is a liability.
maintenance_evidence: Verified via the GitHub API 2026-11-17 as live and non-archived with continuing but modest development. Classified stable-low: the tool is maintained, but its effectiveness is constrained by external source availability rather than by code activity.
licence: GPL-2.0 (project licensing — confirm from the repository licence file)
model_or_data_licence: Third-party sources have their own terms.
licence_restrictions: Copyleft on the tool. The weightier obligations are data-protection ones attaching to harvested personal data.
costs: No fee. Several sources require API keys, some paid (not priced here). Negligible compute.
privacy: Queries disclose the target domain to many third parties. More significantly, the output is a collection of other people's personal data, which makes you a data controller with the obligations that follow.
alternatives: subfinder plus certificate transparency for infrastructure only, avoiding the personal-data collection
Photon for site-specific contact harvesting
Manual research for the handful of people who actually matter to the story
blockers: Harvested email addresses are regulated personal data requiring a retention and protection decision
summary: Reconnaissance tool that gathers names, email addresses, subdomains, hosts and open ports for a domain from search engines…
additional_costs_note: optional paid hosting / commercial licence; self-hosted infrastructure
